prize_parts.citation: For establishing liquid-liquid phase separation and multivalent interactions as a physical-chemical principle organizing the interior of cells into membraneless compartments

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation brought thermodynamics, phase behaviour and multivalent interactions into cell biology and gave a general concept of molecular organisation that did not exist before 2009. Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules behave as liquids, and Rosen supplied the quantitative multivalent-polymer framework that made the idea a physical chemistry rather than a descriptive observation. The concept now shapes work on nucleoli, stress granules, signalling assemblies, neurodegeneration and synthetic condensates, and it has been independently reproduced for about fifteen years. It also answers the question of whether physical chemistry of life, and not only synthesis and tools, is represented in the prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the physiological relevance of many in vitro droplets is still debated, and that an intracellular body being liquid-like is not the same as it being functionally phase separated. Credit is also spread over at least five contributors, so any triple omits Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar and experimental work is substantial. A reasonable committee could also call this cell biology rather than chemistry.

responses.point: Daniel ranks B007 third and says there is no obvious unique trio, and that part of the field is still maturing in vivo.
responses.response: I agree that the trio is not unique and that Pappu and Mittag are a real loss, so I treat this as the weakest point of my case. I still think the P-granule demonstration plus the multivalency framework is the decisive core that the community itself cites, and the in vivo debate concerns which assemblies are phase separated, not whether the physical principle is valid. That is the maturity standard I would apply, and I think it is met. I do not agree that this is a reason to rank it below genetic code expansion, whose concept is also mature but less general.

responses.point: Johan ranks base editing first and argues that a single-laureate prize for David Liu is defensible and cleaner than adding names.
responses.response: I accept that Liu's contribution to base editing is the clearest attribution on the list, and I see why that appeals. My concern is conceptual: base editing is an excellent chemical application on top of the CRISPR platform recognised in 2020, so the novelty of the underlying idea is narrower than in a new organising principle. I would also resist the argument that a clean attribution by itself outweighs breadth of concept. I keep it as an alternative, not as my first choice.

responses.point: Peter puts Gray and Winkler on long-range electron transfer first, and sees B007 as strong but with debate over what is truly phase separated and an allocation that is contested.
responses.response: I share his regard for the Gray and Winkler work, which is exactly the kind of quantitative physical principle I value, and its attribution is cleaner than mine. My reservation is that Marcus theory was recognised in 1992 and the protein tunnelling work extends a known framework, whereas phase separation opened a new way to think about cellular organisation. I agree with him that the in-cell interpretation is still evolving, and that is why I would credit the physical-chemical framework rather than specific functional claims in the citation.

responses.point: Andrei ranks base editing first and sees it as one of the cleanest cases of nucleotide chemistry reshaping biology, with timely maturity.
responses.response: I agree that deaminase chemistry is elegant and the three-person Liu, Komor and Gaudelli attribution is coherent. Where I differ is on whether the lead-trainee structure of a prize carries the same weight as three independent founders of a field, and on the Nishida and Kondo priority question that he flags but does not resolve. I would be comfortable with base editing if the committee settles that, but I do not think it clearly outranks a general concept.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges that the physiological-relevance debate leaves the field mature enough for a prize.
Whether Pappu and Mittag should displace one of the three, or whether a three-person cut is acceptable.
Whether the committee will see this as chemistry rather than cell biology.
Whether Hyman and Brangwynne and Rosen can be framed as one achievement, or the Rosen framework is better treated separately.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I am a Lund colleague of Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai and work in lipid and amyloid assembly, which is adjacent to condensates, but I have no personal tie to the candidates named.
